section.title: The Exodus from Egypt
section.sectionRationale: This is the hinge of the whole book: the plague falls exactly as foretold, Pharaoh finally lets Israel go, and after four hundred and thirty years of sojourning a mixed multitude walks free. The Passover statute is then fixed for every generation to come.
section.thesis: At midnight the LORD strikes Egypt's firstborn and Pharaoh drives Israel out; the people leave in haste, plundering Egypt as promised, and the LORD seals the Passover as a lasting statute for native and foreigner alike who join themselves to Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the midnight judgment and Pharaoh's urgent release of Israel; the actual departure, the plunder, and the note on the four hundred and thirty years; and the closing statutes fixing who may keep the Passover and how.

units.label: Midnight, and Pharaoh releases Israel
units.note: the cry goes up, the sentence executed

verses.text: Now at midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, as well as all the firstborn among the livestock.
During the night Pharaoh got up, he and all his officials and all the Egyptians, and there was loud wailing in Egypt; for there was no house without someone dead.
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, “Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested.
Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart! And bless me also.”
And in order to send them out of the land quickly, the Egyptians urged the people on. “For otherwise,” they said, “we are all going to die!”

units.label: The departure and the plunder
units.note: 430 years, and the LORD's divisions go out

verses.text: So the people took their dough before it was leavened, carrying it on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing.
Furthermore, the Israelites acted on Moses' word and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing.
And the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request. In this way they plundered the Egyptians.
The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth with about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children.
And a {{mixed|mixed}} multitude also went up with them, along with great droves of livestock, both flocks and herds.

Since their dough had no leaven, the people baked what they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened loaves. For when they had been driven out of Egypt, they could not delay and had not prepared any provisions for themselves.
Now the duration of the Israelites' stay in Egypt was 430 years.
At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD's divisions went out of the land of Egypt.

Because the LORD kept a {{vigil|vigil}} that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt, this same night is to be a vigil to the LORD, to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come.

units.label: Statutes for the Passover
units.note: who may eat it, and how

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the statute of the Passover: No foreigner is to eat of it.
But any slave who has been purchased may eat of it, after you have circumcised him.
A temporary resident or hired hand shall not eat the Passover.
It must be eaten inside one house. You are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you may not break any of the bones.
The whole congregation of Israel must celebrate it.

If a {{foreigner|foreigner}} resides with you and wants to celebrate the LORD's Passover, all the males in the household must be circumcised; then he may come near to celebrate it, and he shall be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised man may eat of it.
The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner who resides among you.”
Then all the Israelites did this, they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.
And on that very day the LORD brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.

mixed.gloss: A mixed multitude, a great mixture of non-Israelites who left Egypt along with Israel. From the very night of the exodus, God's people include those grafted in from outside, foreshadowing a redeemed people not limited to physical descent from Abraham.

vigil.gloss: A night of watching, guarding, keeping vigil. The LORD Himself kept watch that night to bring Israel out, and Israel is then called to keep the same night as an act of watchful remembrance every year.

foreigner.gloss: A resident foreigner living among Israel. The law makes room for such a person to join the covenant people fully through circumcision, showing that the boundary of Israel was never simply ethnic but covenantal, open to whoever would be joined to the LORD.

basic.context: This is the night Israel actually leaves Egypt. The plague falls exactly as warned, Pharaoh finally breaks and lets the people go, and Israel walks out with plunder from the very people who enslaved them, four hundred and thirty years after they first went down to Egypt.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real historical departure at a fixed point in time; it is not a template for how to treat employers or neighbors today. The rules about who may eat the Passover describe Israel's specific covenant boundary, later opened fully in Christ to all nations without requiring circumcision, Galatians 3.
basic.originalLanguages: A mixed multitude, erev rav, leaves Egypt alongside Israel, hinting that God's people were never purely one ethnic line. The LORD keeps shimurim, a vigil, that night, and calls Israel to keep the same watch every year after. And the ger, the resident foreigner, could be joined fully to Israel through circumcision, on the same terms as any native.
basic.typology: The four hundred and thirty years ending to the very day shows God's precision in keeping His promises on His own timetable. The mixed multitude leaving with Israel anticipates a people of God gathered from every nation, not limited to physical descent, fulfilled in the church, Galatians 3:28-29.
basic.christ: The unbroken bones of the Passover lamb, fixed as law in verse 46, are fulfilled exactly at the cross, John 19:36, where Jesus' legs are not broken though the other two crucified beside Him have theirs broken. The precise timing of deliverance points to a God who keeps every promise to the day, as He will keep His promise of Christ's return.
basic.god: God is exactingly faithful, bringing Israel out on the very day the 430 years were complete, and He is also generous, opening the door of covenant belonging to any foreigner willing to be joined to His people through the appointed sign. Judgment and welcome sit side by side in this chapter.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 3:16, 3:28-29 speak of a mixed people, Jew and Gentile, united in Christ, the true seed of Abraham. John 19:36 fulfills the unbroken bones of the Passover lamb. Genesis 15:13-14 had already foretold 400 years of affliction, fulfilled here precisely.
basic.oneStory: God keeps His ancient promise to the day, judges the oppressor, and brings out a people that already includes those from beyond Israel's bloodline. This is the pattern the whole Bible completes: a people gathered from every nation, redeemed by a lamb, walking out of bondage into freedom in Christ.

context.literary:
After twenty-eight verses of instruction the narrative finally releases the blow it has been holding back since Exodus 11:4. It does so in a single sentence, verse 29, with no description of the destroyer and no detail of the deaths. The narrator is restrained where we might expect drama, and the restraint is itself solemn. What follows moves quickly: Pharaoh rises in the night, summons Moses, and gives in completely, verses 30 to 32. The pace matches the haste the Passover had anticipated, and verse 39 ties the two together by explaining the unleavened bread through the speed of the departure.

The passage closes a long series of reversals. In Exodus 10:28 Pharaoh had told Moses 'never see my face again'; now he summons him by night. In Exodus 5:2 he had said 'I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go'; now he says 'Go, worship the LORD as you have requested,' verse 31. He had bargained over the children in Exodus 10:10-11 and over the flocks in Exodus 10:24; now he releases 'both you and the Israelites' and adds 'take your flocks and herds as well,' verse 32. Every earlier condition is withdrawn. Exodus 11:1 had said he would 'drive you out completely,' and verse 39 uses the same language: they 'had been driven out of Egypt.'

The narrative then slows into a travel notice and a summary, verses 37 to 42, with a place of departure, a number, a mixed company, and a span of years. The phrase 'to the very day' in verse 41 and 'on that very day' in verse 51 frame the section and link it to the same phrase in verse 17. Between them stands a final block of law, verses 43 to 49, the statute of who may eat the Passover. The chapter thus ends where it began, with the Passover, but now looking outward to those not born in Israel. Verse 50 repeats the obedience formula of verse 28, and verse 51 restates verse 41, so that the whole chapter is bracketed by command, obedience and deliverance.
context.historical:
The departure begins at Rameses, verse 37, one of the two store cities Israel had built with forced labour, Exodus 1:11. The people who had been made to build it now march out of it. Succoth, the first stop, means 'booths' or 'shelters,' as the BSB footnote notes. Numbers 33:3-5 retells the same day: they set out 'on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after the Passover' and 'marched out defiantly in full view of all the Egyptians, who were burying all their firstborn.'

The date of the exodus is debated. 1 Kings 6:1 places Solomon's temple 'in the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt,' which many take to point to the fifteenth century BC. Others note the city name Rameses and argue for the thirteenth century, reading the 480 years as a round figure. The text itself is more concerned with God's timing than with ours: 'at the end of the 430 years, to the very day,' verse 41.

The 430 years themselves raise a textual question. The BSB footnote records that the Samaritan Pentateuch reads 'in Canaan and Egypt' and the Septuagint 'in Egypt and Canaan,' which would count the patriarchs' time in Canaan within the total. Paul says the law came '430 years' after the covenant with Abraham, Galatians 3:17, which fits that longer reckoning.

The asking of verse 35 was not borrowing, as some older English versions suggested, but a request. Egypt, struck and afraid, gave freely, and Psalm 105:38 says 'Egypt was glad when they departed.' The silver and gold would later be given for the tabernacle, Exodus 35:22, and misused for the golden calf, Exodus 32:2-4. The 'mixed multitude' of verse 38 was likely made up of other oppressed peoples and Egyptians who had come to fear the LORD after the plagues, compare Exodus 9:20.
context.canonical:
The midnight judgment and the departure are recalled throughout Scripture. Psalm 78:51, 105:36 and 135:8 recount the striking of the firstborn, and Psalm 105:37 adds that 'He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled.' Psalm 136:10-11 places both acts in the refrain of the LORD's loving devotion. Israel's creeds rehearse the event, Deuteronomy 6:21 and 26:8, and the prophets build their hopes on it: 'When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son,' Hosea 11:1.

The plunder of Egypt answers Genesis 15:14, 'afterward they will depart with many possessions,' and Exodus 3:21-22, 'you will not go away empty-handed.' The law then turns Israel's experience into a rule for its own slaves: a released servant must not be sent away empty-handed, 'Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt,' Deuteronomy 15:13-15.

The statute on foreigners is developed later. Numbers 9:14 repeats that the same Passover statute applies to foreigner and native. Leviticus 19:34 commands Israel to love the foreigner 'as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.' Isaiah 56:3-7 promises that foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will be brought to His holy mountain, for 'My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.' Individual outsiders who joined Israel, Rahab, Joshua 6:25, Ruth, Ruth 1:16, and Caleb the Kenizzite, Numbers 32:12, show the door of verse 48 standing open.

The New Testament takes up these threads. Matthew applies Hosea 11:1 to Jesus, Matthew 2:15. Luke describes His coming death as His exodos, His 'departure,' Luke 9:31. John sees the rule of verse 46 fulfilled at the cross, John 19:36. Paul uses the 430 years to argue that the law cannot annul the promise, Galatians 3:17. And Ephesians 2:12-19 describes Gentiles once 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel' who are now 'fellow citizens with the saints,' brought near 'through the blood of Christ.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that the exodus happened exactly as God had said it would. The midnight of verse 29 answers the 'about midnight' of Exodus 11:4. The firstborn of Pharaoh on his throne is named in both places. The asking for silver and gold was commanded in Exodus 3:22 and 11:2, and the favour God gave is recorded in verse 36. Even the span of years matches a count, verse 41. Every detail says that the LORD's word does not fail.

He also wanted Israel to understand that its freedom was not won by negotiation or rebellion. Pharaoh did not grant liberty as a concession; he was broken. The Israelites did not fight their way out; they were driven out by the Egyptians themselves, verse 33. Their unleavened bread was a reminder that they had left before they were ready, carried along by what God was doing.

And he wanted them to know who belonged to the redeemed community. The statute in verses 43 to 49 does two things at once. It closes the table to those who stand outside the covenant, and it opens it to any foreigner who will take the covenant sign. The people who had just walked out of Egypt as foreigners were being taught how to receive foreigners among themselves.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this passage is narrative. The death of the firstborn, the plunder, the route from Rameses and the number of the people describe what happened once, and they are not models to be copied. Reading the plunder as licence to take what belongs to others, or the midnight strike as a pattern for human vengeance, ignores that these were acts of God in fulfilment of His own word and His judgment on Egypt's long oppression.

Verses 42 to 49 are prescriptive for Israel. The night is to be kept as a vigil for all generations, and the Passover is limited to the circumcised. Under the new covenant the boundary marker changes. Paul insists that Gentiles need not be circumcised to belong to God's people, Galatians 5:2-6, and that true circumcision is 'a matter of the heart, by the Spirit,' Romans 2:29. What carries over is the principle of verse 49: 'The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner.' In Christ there is one table and one people, and no one belongs by birth alone.

debates.question: What is the significance of the mixed multitude leaving with Israel?

views.label: A picture of the eventual inclusion of the nations
views.case: Even at the founding exodus, non-Israelites join God's redeemed people. The statute of verses 48 and 49 gives them a way to belong fully, and later figures such as Rahab, Ruth and Caleb the Kenizzite show the door standing open. The exodus community was never defined by bloodline alone.

views.label: A source of later trouble
views.case: Numbers 11:4 speaks of 'the rabble among them' who had 'a strong craving for other food,' and many readers connect that group with the multitude of Exodus 12:38. Their presence, though not condemned here, contributed to the grumbling of the wilderness years.

debates.bearing: Both readings can be held together. Inclusion of outsiders is a genuine grace, yet belonging to God's people always calls for full covenant commitment, not mere proximity, which is exactly why verses 43 to 49 follow directly after verse 38.

debates.question: Do the 430 years of verse 40 cover only the time in Egypt, or the patriarchs' time in Canaan as well?

views.label: A long stay of 430 years in Egypt
views.case: The Hebrew text reads 'the duration of the Israelites' stay in Egypt was 430 years,' and Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6 speak of four hundred years of affliction in a land not their own. On this view the round 400 and the exact 430 describe the same long sojourn.

views.label: A combined period in Canaan and Egypt
views.case: The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint, as the BSB footnote records, include Canaan in the count. Paul reckons 430 years from the promise to Abraham to the law, Galatians 3:17. The genealogy of Exodus 6:16-20, where Moses is only the fourth generation from Levi, and 'the fourth generation' of Genesis 15:16 are also thought to fit a shorter stay in Egypt.

debates.bearing: The point of the verse does not depend on the answer. Whether the count begins with Jacob's descent or with Abraham's call, it ends 'to the very day,' verse 41, and the emphasis falls on God's exact faithfulness to His timetable.

debates.question: How should the 600,000 men of verse 37 be understood?

views.label: A literal count
views.case: The figure is consistent across the Pentateuch: 603,550 in Exodus 38:26 and Numbers 1:46, and 600,000 on foot in Numbers 11:21. Exodus 38:25-26 ties the number to a precise total of silver collected, half a shekel per man. On this view the whole nation, with women and children, numbered well over two million, and the wilderness provision is presented as a sustained miracle.

views.label: Units rather than individuals
views.case: The Hebrew word for 'thousand,' elef, can also mean a clan or military unit, and some suggest the census lists count such units, giving a much smaller population. They point to the practical difficulties of a vast company in the Sinai and to Moses' reminder that Israel was 'the fewest of all peoples,' Deuteronomy 7:7.

debates.bearing: The consistency of the figures in the text is real and should be taken seriously, and any alternative has to explain Exodus 38:25-26. Either way the point of verse 37 is that the promise of Exodus 1:7 had come true: the family of seventy had become a great people.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'loud wailing' of verse 30 is tse'aqah gedolah, 'a great cry,' the phrase Moses had used in Exodus 11:6. The noun is the same one used for Israel's cry under slavery: 'I have heard them crying out,' Exodus 3:7, and 'the cry of the Israelites has reached Me,' Exodus 3:9. The measure is exact. The cry that Egypt caused in Israel now rises from every Egyptian house.

In verse 35 the people 'asked,' sha'al, the ordinary verb for making a request. It does not mean borrowing with a promise to return, and nothing in the text suggests deception. Verse 36 then says 'they plundered the Egyptians,' using the verb natsal in an intensive stem, 'to strip.' The same root in another stem means 'to deliver' or 'rescue,' and God used it in Exodus 6:6, 'I will... deliver you from their bondage.' The wordplay is pointed. The God who delivers Israel from Egypt also lets Israel strip Egypt, and the language of salvation and spoil comes from one root. The fulfilment of Exodus 3:21, 'you will not go away empty-handed,' uses reqam, 'empty,' the same word that Deuteronomy 15:13 uses for a released slave who must not be sent away empty-handed.

The 'mixed multitude' of verse 38 is erev rav. Erev comes from a root meaning 'to mix,' and it describes people of mixed or foreign origin in Nehemiah 13:3, 'all of foreign descent,' and Jeremiah 25:20, 'all the mixed tribes.'

The 'divisions' of verses 41 and 51 are tseva'ot, 'hosts' or 'armies.' Exodus 6:26 and 7:4 had already called Israel 'My divisions, My people.' The same noun stands in the title 'the LORD of Hosts,' 1 Samuel 1:3. A slave people leaves Egypt described as the army of the LORD.

The 'vigil' of verse 42 is shimmurim, from shamar, 'to watch' or 'to keep.' The phrase appears twice in the verse: the LORD kept a night of watching to bring Israel out, and Israel is to keep a night of watching for Him. The same verb stands behind 'keep the Feast,' verse 17, and 'keep this command,' verse 24, and Psalm 121:4 calls the LORD the 'Protector of Israel,' the one who keeps watch and 'will neither slumber nor sleep.'

Finally, the statute of verses 43 to 49 uses a precise vocabulary for outsiders. The ben-nekar, literally 'son of a foreign land,' verse 43, is the foreigner who remains outside. The toshav and the sakir of verse 45 are the temporary resident and the hired worker, people living among Israel without joining it. The ger of verse 48 is the resident foreigner who has settled among the people, and he may become 'like a native,' ezrach, of the land. Israel knew the word well. Moses named his son Gershom because 'I have become a foreigner in a foreign land,' Exodus 2:22, and God had told Abram that his descendants would be 'strangers,' gerim, in a land not their own, Genesis 15:13.

typology.type: Israel, God's firstborn son, brought out of Egypt
typology.fulfillment: The LORD had told Pharaoh, 'Israel is My firstborn son... let My son go,' Exodus 4:22-23, and the night of verse 29 is the fulfilment of that warning. Hosea recalls it: 'out of Egypt I called My son,' Hosea 11:1. Matthew applies the verse to Jesus returning from Egypt as a child, Matthew 2:15, presenting Him as the true Son who relives Israel's story and succeeds where Israel failed. The type falls short because Israel was a son by adoption and often disobedient, while Jesus is the eternal Son in whom the Father is well pleased, Matthew 3:17.

typology.type: The exodus as departure through death to freedom
typology.fulfillment: Israel's exodus came on the night of death and led out of bondage toward the land of promise. Luke describes Moses and Elijah speaking with Jesus about 'His departure,' exodos, 'which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31. Jesus' death and resurrection are His exodus, and through it He leads His people out of the dominion of darkness, Colossians 1:13. The escalation is that Israel left one tyrant and one land, while Christ breaks the power of death itself, Hebrews 2:14-15, and leads His people into an inheritance that cannot perish, 1 Peter 1:4.

Israel left enriched by the very people who had enslaved it, and much of that wealth was later offered for the tabernacle, Exodus 35:22. Paul applies Psalm 68:18, a psalm that celebrates God's march from Sinai, to Christ's ascension: 'He led captives away, and gave gifts to men,' Ephesians 4:8. The spoils of His victory are given to His people for the building of His church, Ephesians 4:11-12. The type falls short because Egypt's gold could be turned into an idol, Exodus 32:4, while the gifts of the ascended Christ build up His body in truth and love.

typology.type: The foreigner who joins the Passover through circumcision
typology.fulfillment: A foreigner could come near the table and become 'like a native of the land' if his household received the covenant sign, verse 48. The New Testament opens the door fully. Gentiles once 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' have been 'brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:12-13, and are 'no longer strangers and foreigners,' Ephesians 2:19. The sign that admits them is the circumcision 'performed by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11. The escalation is that belonging is no longer an exception granted to a few but the calling of every nation, Revelation 7:9.

typology.type: The lamb whose bones are not broken, verse 46
typology.fulfillment: The Passover lamb was to be eaten whole and within one house, and none of its bones broken. John sees this fulfilled when the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, John 19:33, and cites the Scripture, 'Not one of His bones will be broken,' John 19:36, a text that echoes both this verse and Psalm 34:20, where the LORD 'protects all his bones.' The detail identifies Jesus as the true Passover lamb and as the righteous sufferer whom God preserves, though the type falls short in that the lamb stayed dead and Jesus rose.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the theme of the firstborn son. The whole contest with Pharaoh was framed by Exodus 4:22-23: Israel is God's firstborn, and if Pharaoh will not release him, Pharaoh's firstborn will die. Verse 29 is that sentence carried out. The New Testament presents Jesus as the Son in whom Israel's sonship is fulfilled. Matthew takes Hosea 11:1, 'out of Egypt I called My son,' and applies it to Jesus, Matthew 2:15, so that His life begins by tracing Israel's path. Yet the pattern is also reversed. In Egypt the firstborn of the enemy died so that God's firstborn could go free. At the cross God's own firstborn, 'the firstborn over all creation,' Colossians 1:15, dies, and by His death His enemies are reconciled, Romans 5:10.

It leads to Christ through His own exodus. Luke says that on the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus 'about His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31. The Greek word is exodos. The deliverance of Exodus 12 was accomplished by God on a single night; the greater deliverance would be accomplished by Jesus in Jerusalem, at Passover, through His death and resurrection. As Israel went out from Rameses, the city of its forced labour, so believers are rescued 'from the dominion of darkness' and brought 'into the kingdom of His beloved Son,' Colossians 1:13.

It leads to Christ through the statute of verse 46. The Passover lamb was not to have a bone broken. John saw the soldiers spare Jesus' legs and wrote, 'these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled,' John 19:36. The law given on the night Israel left Egypt was kept, to the letter, at the cross.

It leads to Christ through the welcome of the foreigner. Verses 48 and 49 made room for the outsider to eat the Passover as a native. Jesus spoke of 'other sheep that are not of this fold,' who would become 'one flock' with 'one shepherd,' John 10:16. Paul says that the dividing wall has been broken down and that Jew and Gentile have been made 'one new man' through the cross, Ephesians 2:14-16. The mixed multitude of verse 38 is a small beginning; the multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' standing before the Lamb is its end, Revelation 7:9.

There is also a contrast worth noticing. Verse 42 says the LORD kept watch over Israel through the night of the exodus. On the night before His own exodus, Jesus asked His disciples to watch with Him, and they slept: 'Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?' Matthew 26:40. The Gospels draw no explicit line to Exodus 12:42, so this is a thematic echo rather than a declared fulfilment, but it is striking. God had watched for His people, and when the Son kept His vigil, His people could not keep it with Him. He went out alone to accomplish the departure that would bring them home.
study.god:
The chapter first shows God as the one whose word governs history. What He announced in Exodus 11:4-6 happens at midnight in verse 29. What He promised to Abram in Genesis 15:14, and to Moses in Exodus 3:21-22, happens in verses 35 and 36. What He counted in years ends 'to the very day,' verse 41. God does not merely foresee events; He brings them to pass at the time He appointed.

It shows Him as the judge who is not partial. The plague reached from 'the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon,' verse 29. The highest and the lowest in Egypt stood under the same sentence. Royal power did not protect Pharaoh's son, and the lowest status did not exempt the prisoner's. Every house in Egypt found that judgment was no respecter of persons, verse 30.

It shows Him as sovereign over hearts. 'The LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians,' verse 36. The same Egyptians who had oppressed Israel for generations now load them with gifts. Scripture elsewhere says 'the king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD,' Proverbs 21:1, and here a whole nation's goodwill is turned by His hand. Even Pharaoh, who had refused to know the LORD, asks for a blessing, verse 32.

It shows Him as the God who watches. Verse 42 says the LORD kept vigil that night. He is not a distant power who acts and withdraws, but one who stays awake over His people through the darkest night of their history. The call for Israel to keep the same vigil every year is a call to share His watchfulness, remembering the night He did not sleep.

It shows Him as holy and welcoming at once. He sets clear boundaries around His table, verses 43 to 45, because the Passover belongs to those in covenant with Him. But He also provides a way in for the foreigner, verse 48, and insists on one law for native and outsider, verse 49. The same God who distinguished between Egypt and Israel does not make ethnicity the final line. The line is covenant with Him.

For worship, this chapter calls for confidence and humility together. Confidence, because the God who kept His word to the very day will keep every promise He has made. Humility, because Israel contributed nothing to its release but obedience. The people who walked out 'by their divisions,' verse 51, marched as an army that had not fought, carrying bread they had not had time to prepare, rich with gifts they had not earned.

crossReferences.note: The LORD's first message to Pharaoh names Israel His firstborn son and warns, 'since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son!' Exodus 12:29 is the fulfilment of that warning. The whole plague narrative is framed as a contest over God's firstborn.

Moses had announced the plague 'about midnight,' naming the firstborn of Pharaoh on his throne and promising a great cry such as had never been heard. Verses 29 and 30 repeat the language almost word for word, showing that the LORD did exactly what He said, down to the hour and the sound of grief.

God told Abram his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own, enslaved four hundred years, and that God would judge that nation and 'afterward they will depart with many possessions.' Exodus 12:35-41 fulfils each part: the long sojourn, the judgment, and the departure with silver and gold.

At the burning bush God promised that Israel would not go away empty-handed but would ask for silver, gold and clothing and so plunder the Egyptians. Exodus 12:35-36 records the same asking, the same favour and the same verb for plunder, closing the circle opened at Horeb.

The wilderness itinerary retells the departure: Israel set out from Rameses the day after the Passover and 'marched out defiantly in full view of all the Egyptians, who were burying all their firstborn,' because the LORD had judged their gods. It adds the picture of Egypt burying its dead as Israel left.

A released Hebrew slave must not be sent away empty-handed but furnished liberally, because 'you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you.' Israel's own exodus, when it left Egypt laden with gifts, becomes the pattern for how it must treat those it releases.

Paul argues that the law 'that came 430 years later' cannot annul the covenant God made with Abraham. He uses the figure of Exodus 12:40-41 to show that promise came first and law second, so that the inheritance rests on promise and not on the law.

The soldiers break the legs of the two crucified with Jesus but not His, and John cites the Scripture, 'Not one of His bones will be broken.' The rule of Exodus 12:46 for the Passover lamb is kept at the cross, marking Jesus as the lamb of the true Passover.

Foreigners who join themselves to the LORD are told not to fear exclusion. They will be brought to His holy mountain, their sacrifices accepted, 'for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.' The narrow door of Exodus 12:48 widens into a prophetic vision of the nations gathered.

Gentiles who were once 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel' and 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' are now 'brought near through the blood of Christ' and are 'no longer strangers and foreigners.' Exodus 12:48-49 made the foreigner like a native; Christ makes Gentiles fellow citizens.

Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak with Jesus about 'His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.' The word is exodos. The Lord's death and resurrection are presented as a new and greater exodus, with Moses himself present to speak of it.

The psalm recalls the striking of Egypt's firstborn, then says 'He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled,' and 'Egypt was glad when they departed.' It confirms that the gifts of Exodus 12:35-36 were given freely by a nation afraid of Israel's God.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture had been waiting for this night since Genesis 15. God had told Abram that his offspring would be strangers and slaves, and that He would judge their oppressor and bring them out. Genesis closed with Joseph's bones in a coffin in Egypt, and Exodus opened with a people multiplying under a king who did not know Joseph. Exodus 12:29-51 is the long promise kept. The family of seventy that went down into Egypt comes up as a host of hundreds of thousands, with a crowd of others among them.

The chapter also answers the old question of Genesis 12:3. God had said that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abram. Here the first sign of that blessing appears in an unlikely place: a mixed multitude attaches itself to Israel, and the law immediately makes room for foreigners to share the Passover. Even Pharaoh, in his defeat, asks Moses to bless him, verse 32. The exodus is not only Israel's story; it is the start of God's plan for the nations.

What follows builds on this night. The firstborn will be claimed, Exodus 13. The sea will be crossed, Exodus 14. At Sinai the redeemed people will receive the law that begins, 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery,' Exodus 20:2. Throughout the Old Testament the exodus is the measure of God's power and faithfulness, and when Israel later goes into exile, the prophets promise a new exodus, greater than the first.

That new exodus comes in Christ. He is the Son called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15. He accomplishes His exodus at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, at Passover, as the Lamb whose bones are not broken, John 19:36. Through Him the people of God are drawn from Jew and Gentile alike into one body, the fulfilment of the one law for native and foreigner.

The story ends with a greater departure and a greater arrival. The people who were once strangers everywhere will have a home, and the multitude from every nation will stand before the throne and before the Lamb, Revelation 7:9. The night of watching will give way to a city where 'there will be no more night,' Revelation 22:5, because the God who kept vigil over His people will dwell with them in unending light.

quiz.q: What finally moved Pharaoh to let Israel go?

options.text: The death of every firstborn in Egypt at midnight, including his own household.
options.note: Verses 29 to 31 show this was the decisive, terrible blow.

options.text: A personal request from Moses' father-in-law.
options.note: Jethro plays no role in this chapter; the tenth plague is what breaks Pharaoh.

options.text: Pharaoh had a change of heart on his own, unrelated to any plague.
options.note: The text ties his release directly to the plague of the firstborn, not an independent change of heart.

options.text: The Israelites overpowered the Egyptian army.
options.note: There is no battle here; Pharaoh releases Israel because of the plague, not military defeat.

quiz.q: How long had Israel's stay in Egypt lasted, according to verse 40?

options.text: 430 years, ending to the very day.
options.note: The text is precise about both the length and the exactness of its fulfillment.

options.text: 40 years.
options.note: 40 years describes the later wilderness wandering, not the Egyptian sojourn.

options.text: 70 years.
options.note: 70 is the number of Jacob's household that first went down to Egypt, Exodus 1:5, not the length of the stay.

options.text: The text gives no length of time.
options.note: Verse 40 states the figure plainly, 430 years.

quiz.q: Who left Egypt alongside the Israelites, according to verse 38?

options.text: A mixed multitude of non-Israelites, along with great droves of livestock.
options.note: The text explicitly notes this mixed group leaving with Israel.

options.text: Only ethnic Israelites, with no outsiders at all.
options.note: The text specifically mentions a mixed multitude joining the departure.

options.text: Pharaoh's own army, escorting them to the border.
options.note: There is no escort by Pharaoh's army; Egypt urged them to leave quickly out of fear.

options.text: No livestock, only people.
options.note: Great droves of both flocks and herds are explicitly mentioned leaving with the people.

quiz.q: Under what condition could a foreigner join in eating the Passover, according to verses 48 to 49?

options.text: All the males in his household had to be circumcised, making him like a native of the land.
options.note: This is the exact condition given, opening full covenant participation to any who would be circumcised.

options.text: No foreigner could ever eat the Passover under any circumstance.
options.note: The text explicitly allows for a foreigner to join through circumcision, contradicting a total exclusion.

options.text: Only payment of a fee was required.
options.note: No fee is mentioned; the requirement is circumcision, joining the covenant sign.

options.text: Any visitor, regardless of status, could freely eat it.
options.note: Verse 45 explicitly excludes a mere temporary resident or hired hand from eating it without the covenant sign.

quiz.q: What detail of the Passover lamb in this chapter is later fulfilled at the cross?

options.text: That none of its bones would be broken.
options.note: Verse 46 is fulfilled literally in Jesus at the cross, John 19:36.

options.text: That it must be eaten with bitter herbs.
options.note: True of the lamb generally, but this is not the detail the New Testament singles out as fulfilled at the cross.

options.text: That it had to be a red heifer.
options.note: The red heifer is a different, unrelated ordinance in Numbers 19.

options.text: No detail from this chapter is echoed in the New Testament.
options.note: John 19:36 explicitly cites the unbroken bones from this Passover instruction.

questions: God kept His 430-year-old promise to the very day. Where do you need to trust His timing on a promise that feels long overdue?

Egypt's own goods went out with Israel as a form of restitution for years of forced labor. Where might God be calling you to trust Him for provision rather than anxiously grasping for security yourself?

A mixed multitude joined Israel's exodus from the very start. How does it change your view of the church to know that God's people have never been defined by ethnicity or background, but by belonging to Him?

The Passover lamb's unbroken bones point straight to Jesus at the cross. Where do small, seemingly minor details of your life might God also be weaving into a larger, faithful pattern you cannot yet see?

The door to the Passover was open to any foreigner willing to be joined fully to God's people. Who around you needs that same invitation into full belonging in Christ, and are you willing to extend it?

translationNotes.note: 600,000 men on foot likely refers to able-bodied men eligible for military service, meaning the total number of people, including women and children, would have been considerably larger.

The 430 years is counted differently across ancient traditions, some measuring from Jacob's descent into Egypt and others from Abraham's earlier sojourning; the text's own emphasis is on precision and fulfillment, not the details of the calculation.
Not breaking any of its bones may reflect ordinary care in preparing and eating the animal whole, but it becomes theologically loaded once John ties it directly to Jesus at the crucifixion.
